title: Using Multi‐Point Activity Surveys for identifying Daubenton's bat (Myotis daubentonii, Kuhl, 1817) commuting routes and selecting candidate dark corridors: A case study from the West Midlands, UK
content:
Using Multi-Point Activity Surveys to identify common commuting routes and key landscape features used by Daubenton's bats. In this case study from the West Midlands, the survey method sheds light on how and by what routes bats are commuting through a major conurbation.


Abstract

Context. In the complex balance between the landscapes of energy and fear, human artefacts (e.g., lighting, noise and barriers) affect the routes taken by commuting bats. Those effects result in cumulative impacts on bat fitness by altering nightly calorific burden. Little is known about the movements of urban bats, with mitigation efforts seldom being evidence-based. Approach and methods. We applied a field protocol (Multi-Point Activity Survey) combining visual and acoustic observations along riparian corridors in two case studies to quantify and visually represent commuting routes used by Myotis daubentonii in an urban landscape. We hypothesised that MultiPAS data can be used to statistically identify preferred commuting routes along urban canals. Furthermore, we expected that using those data and available aerial imagery can be combined to provide evidence-based identification of candidate dark corridor sites. In these case studies from the West Midlands, UK, we sought to demonstrate the effective application of the method in two survey methods: a linear study and a canal junction study. Results. The linear method identified important bat ingress and egress points, and a key candidate dark corridor site through a residential area. The junction survey method revealed candidate dark corridors at three junctions and a crossing point for the retention of vegetation. The combined data also allowed us to infer the locations of two major feeding areas for bats. Practical implications. We demonstrate the successful application of the MultiPAS method for identifying commuting routes and crossing points for trawling bats. These data can allow for the selection of corridor sites in effective, evidence-based, landscape-scale conservation.
